item.title: USDCAD sellers regain control, but key swing support stands in the way
item.description:
The USDCAD extended to a new high for the year on Friday following the weaker-than-expected Canadian jobs report. However, the breakout could only stretch about 7 pips above the previous yearly high near 1.4292 before reversing lower.

The buyers had their shot. They could not keep the break going.

By Friday’s close, the price had rotated lower. Selling continued on Monday until the pair reached its rising 100- and 200-hour moving averages—the blue and green lines on the chart. Buyers leaned against those levels and pushed the price higher.

That rebound stalled near Monday’s closing level and below the previous yearly high at 1.4292. Today, sellers have taken back control, pushing the pair lower in a more trend-like move. The USDCAD is down about 0.48%, making the Canadian dollar the strongest performer against the US dollar.

Sellers reach the next downside hurdle

The decline has reached the top of a swing area between 1.41922 and 1.4204. That area is defined by swing highs and lows going back to September 29, highlighted by the red numbered circles on the chart.

So far, the price has stalled near the upper boundary at 1.4204.

Sellers have secured a victory with the move below the hourly moving averages. To increase their control, however, they need to break below this swing area and stay below it. That would open the door for further downside momentum toward the next swing area between 1.41297 and 1.4153.

Can buyers defend support again?

If buyers hold this area for a fourth consecutive test, the focus shifts toward a rebound to the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near 1.4250.

Those moving averages become the next upside hurdle. Getting above—and staying above—them would weaken the sellers’ control and bring the yearly high near 1.4298 back into focus.

For now, sellers are enjoying the victory today, but they still have work to do. The 1.41922–1.4204 swing area is where their next test begins.

The trading lesson

A break below the moving averages shifts the short-term bias, but the next support area still matters. Sellers need to see follow-through. Buyers need to see support hold.

Use the swing area to define risk and judge control. Hold support, and buyers have a reason to lean against it. Break below and stay below, and sellers earn another victory.

In the video above, I walk through the failed breakout, today’s move lower, and the levels that will help determine whether sellers can keep the pressure on.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCHF ping-pong's between support and resistance targets
item.description:
The USDCHF has been playing ping-pong between support and resistance over the last six trading days, confined to a range between 0.8290 and 0.8348. That is just 58 pips, with neither buyers nor sellers able to sustain a break.

Yesterday, both extremes were tested. Support held near 0.8291, while resistance near 0.8348 capped the rally into the close.

Today, sellers leaned against that topside resistance in the Asia-Pacific session and pushed the price toward two interim support targets:

  • The 100-hour moving average at 0.8322.

  • The 200-hour moving average at 0.83156.

The low reached 0.8313, briefly dipping below both moving averages before quickly bouncing higher. Sellers had their shot below the moving averages, but could not sustain the break.

That puts the moving averages in focus as the close barometer for buyers and sellers. Stay above both, and buyers have room to push back toward the 0.8348 ceiling. Move below both and stay below, and sellers would take more control, opening the door for another test of support near 0.8290.

For now, the broader range remains intact. The moving averages help traders judge which side has the advantage within that range, but a sustained break of the floor or ceiling is needed to move beyond the ping-pong trading.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Stock market movers today. Bumble, JPMorgan and AI stocks: Why market reactions reversed
item.description:
Stocks reverse after the market opens: Bumble's deal, bank earnings and the AI-chip selloff

October 13, 2026 | U.S. stocks | Market snapshot: 10:35 a.m. ET, using 15-minute-delayed data

A stock can rise on disappointing earnings, fall after encouraging guidance or change direction within minutes of the opening bell. Tuesday's U.S. session illustrates why traders should look beyond the first headline. Bumble's takeover, JPMorgan's earnings recovery, healthcare weakness and a selloff in AI-related hardware all offer different lessons about how markets price expectations.

The common thread is that a news event explains why investors are paying attention, but subsequent price action helps reveal how they are evaluating that news.

1. Bumble stock: when a takeover rumor becomes a confirmed offer

Bumble (BMBL) offers perhaps the clearest example of how a trading opportunity can change overnight.

On Monday, shares of the dating-app company surged nearly 50% following reports that it was discussing a potential take-private transaction.

On Tuesday, speculation became an announced agreement. Ithaca Holdings agreed to acquire Bumble in an all-cash transaction valued at approximately $1.3 billion, offering shareholders $6.05 per share.

Bumble shares traded near $5.95 in the supplied morning snapshot, approximately 56.5% above Monday's close.

But the educational opportunity is not simply another large percentage gain.

It is understanding how the nature of the investment changes once an acquisition price becomes public.

At $5.945, the stock was trading approximately 1.77% below the announced cash consideration.

Why would anyone sell at $5.945 when the proposed buyer is offering $6.05?

Because $6.05 is conditional on completing the transaction. Investors must consider the closing timetable, regulatory and other conditions, the opportunity cost of tying up capital, and the possibility that the deal fails.

That difference is called the merger arbitrage spread. It represents potential gross compensation for assuming the time and risk involved, not a guaranteed return.

What to watch:Transaction documents, closing conditions, expected completion timing and any changes to the agreement. A widening spread could reflect greater perceived risk, a longer expected wait or broader market conditions.

The lesson: A stock trading below an agreed takeover price is not automatically undervalued.

2. JPMorgan: why a disappointing earnings report did not keep shares down

JPMorgan Chase (JPM) reported third-quarter net income of approximately $15.3 billion, with earnings of $5.57 per share against analysts' expectations near $5.93.

Reported revenue was approximately $50.2 billion, below the consensus estimate of $51.23 billion. The bank also disclosed $5.75 in earnings per share excluding a significant item, adding nuance to the headline miss.

The stock initially showed weakness.

An earlier 6:45 a.m. ET premarket observation placed JPM near $324.33, almost 3% below Monday's closing price of $334.30. That particular observation should not automatically be attributed to the earnings announcement without confirming the release timing.

During the regular session, the picture changed.

JPM traded above $344 shortly after the opening bell before retreating to approximately $335.78 by the supplied 10:35 a.m. snapshot. That still represented a gain of around 0.44% against Monday's close.

This raises a useful question: Why might investors buy a stock after an earnings miss?

One possibility is that the market distinguishes between a disappointing headline and the underlying operating performance. Investors may examine whether a shortfall reflects temporary trading conditions, unusual charges or more persistent business weakness.

Another possibility is that the initial selling pressure was excessive relative to what the report ultimately revealed.

Neither explanation can be established from the price reversal alone.

The wider banking sector reinforces the need to examine individual companies.

Goldman Sachs (GS):Shares gained approximately 1.55% in the supplied snapshot after the bank reported EPS of $17.01 and revenue of $18.68 billion.

Wells Fargo (WFC):Shares declined approximately 2.49%, despite the broader banking earnings season showing resilience.

JPMorgan (JPM):After moving from weakness to a modest gain, the bank offers a particularly interesting example of intraday reassessment.

The lesson: An earnings beat or miss is only one part of the story. Expectations, earnings quality and subsequent investor demand can matter just as much.

3. UnitedHealth and Johnson & Johnson: why improving fundamentals can accompany falling shares

Two major healthcare companies illustrate another important distinction.

An earnings report can contain genuinely encouraging information without producing a positive stock-market reaction.

UnitedHealth: better medical-cost control, but a fading initial reaction

UnitedHealth (UNH) reported adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share and raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per share.

Its medical-cost ratio improved to 88.4%, indicating that medical expenses were consuming a smaller share of premium revenue.

This is meaningful because controlling medical expenses is central to an insurer's profitability. Nevertheless, in the supplied morning price snapshot, UNH had reversed an earlier positive premarket response and was trading near $376.40, approximately 0.56% below Monday's close.

There are several possible explanations for such behavior.

Investors might welcome improved cost control while remaining uncertain about future insurance membership, pricing, the performance of Optum or the sustainability of the recovery.

A strong quarterly result does not remove every concern about the next several quarters.

Johnson & Johnson: the difference between reported and adjusted earnings

Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) reported third-quarter revenue of $25.4 billion, representing 5.9% growth, and raised its 2026 guidance.

Yet its financial results also illustrated why investors need to understand the difference between reported and adjusted earnings.

Reported EPS was just $0.09, compared with adjusted EPS of $2.59. Special charges included expenses associated with the proposed talc-litigation resolution and business-development transactions.

JNJ shares were down approximately 4.81% in the supplied snapshot.

Investors also had reason to examine the performance of the company's medical-technology division, where growth and competitive pressures remain important considerations.

These two healthcare companies offer a broader lesson.

Good news is not the same as news that exceeds expectations.

A company can improve operationally while its shares decline if investors were anticipating even better performance or believe future risks remain inadequately addressed.

4. Micron and storage stocks: the AI trade faces a competitive test

The pressure on memory and storage shares deserves attention because it has involved several companies rather than one isolated stock.

In the supplied morning snapshot:

Supplied 10:35 a.m. ET snapshot. Percentage changes are relative to the previous regular-session close, not final daily returns.

One reported catalyst is technological progress at Chinese memory producer ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT.

Reports indicate that CXMT has made advances in denser DRAM memory architecture, potentially improving its ability to compete with established global manufacturers.

DRAM is the short-term working memory used by computers and servers. Improvements in chip density can eventually influence production economics and competition.

However, an important distinction is getting lost when these developments are treated as proof that established memory companies are already losing business.

A technological advance is not the same as verified commercial displacement.

Before drawing that conclusion, investors would need evidence of competitive production costs, successful customer qualification, manufacturing yields, shipment volumes and actual changes in pricing.

There is also an important distinction between Micron and the storage companies.

Micron is primarily exposed to semiconductor memory markets, while Western Digital and Seagate have substantial exposure to hard-disk storage. Their products, competitors and pricing cycles are not identical.

What connects them is their exposure to data infrastructure investment and expectations around AI-related demand.

A selloff can weaken without becoming a recovery

Western Digital and Seagate had both recovered noticeably from their opening lows in the supplied snapshot, even though they remained negative for the session.

This is worth observing.

A stock that falls sharply at the open and then recovers part of its decline is behaving differently from one that continues making fresh lows.

But that improvement does not establish a durable bottom.

What to watch:Whether the shares continue recovering toward their previous closes or whether sellers regain control later in the session.

For longer-term investors, the more consequential questions involve memory and storage demand, capacity expansion, margins, competitive pricing and future free cash flow.

The lesson: Industry-wide selling can be informative, but the underlying businesses still require separate analysis.

5. Microsoft and Meta: the AI trade is not moving in one direction

Not all technology stocks were participating in the weakness.

In the supplied snapshot, Microsoft (MSFT) gained approximately 1.31%, while Meta Platforms (META) advanced approximately 3.33%.

Both were outperforming the Nasdaq-100 ETF, while Micron and several storage companies were moving in the opposite direction.

That divergence suggests investors were not treating every AI-exposed business identically.

One possible interpretation is that investors were differentiating between companies monetizing software, advertising and digital services and hardware businesses exposed to manufacturing cycles, capacity expansion and changing competitive conditions.

However, the distinction should not be overstated.

Microsoft and Meta also spend heavily on AI infrastructure, and the relationship between capital investment and eventual profitability is relevant to their valuations.

A single morning's relative performance does not establish a sustained rotation.

The useful question is whether this divergence persists over several sessions and is supported by business developments, or whether it proves to be temporary positioning.

For traders, relative strength can help identify which stocks are holding up better during broader market weakness.

For investors, it is only the beginning of the analysis. Business quality, valuation and expected cash generation still matter.

What traders should watch during the rest of Tuesday's session

Rather than trying to predict every stock's next move, traders can use the previous closing price as an initial reference for evaluating whether the market is accepting or rejecting the latest news.

JPM

$334.30

JPMorgan: Can the recovery survive?

Sustained trading above Monday's close would keep the recovery intact relative to that reference. A renewed move below it would weaken the immediate interpretation.

UNH

$378.52

UnitedHealth: Can buyers restore the positive reaction?

A recovery above the previous close would improve the immediate picture, while continued weakness would suggest investors remain unconvinced.

MU

$989.04

Micron: Is the semiconductor selloff stabilizing?

Watch whether buyers can recover some of the decline and whether the broader semiconductor sector participates.

WDC / STX

$386.94 / $753.25

Western Digital and Seagate: Can the rebounds develop?

A recovery toward their respective Monday closes would indicate improving price action, but sustained demand matters more than a brief bounce.

BMBL

$6.05

Bumble: The acquisition price is the key reference

Unlike the other stocks, the central question is whether the agreed transaction closes, rather than whether a normal earnings-driven price recovery continues.

All reference levels above are supplied October 12, 2026, regular-session closes, except Bumble's announced acquisition consideration. They are analytical reference points, not recommended entries, targets or stop-loss orders.

There is an important difference between the time horizons here.

A day trader may find a recovery above the previous close useful for assessing intraday demand. A longer-term investor should not mistake that recovery for confirmation that a company's business outlook or valuation has improved.

The reverse is also true. One difficult session does not necessarily undermine a sound long-term investment case.

The bigger lesson: markets trade expectations, not headlines

Tuesday's action reminds us that a stock's price reaction depends on more than the apparent quality of the news.

JPMorgan's recovery suggests that investors were willing to reconsider its earnings miss. UnitedHealth and Johnson & Johnson illustrate why stronger guidance or encouraging operational results may still fail to satisfy expectations.

Micron and the storage companies show how competitive developments can trigger concern across an industry, even before their full commercial consequences are known.

And Bumble illustrates something different again: once a takeover price is announced, the investment question changes from speculation about an offer to assessing the transaction's completion risk.

The opening price is information. It is not necessarily the market's final judgment.

For traders, watching how price behaves after the opening reaction can reveal whether that response is strengthening, weakening or being reversed.

For investors, those moves can identify questions worth investigating, but they should be considered alongside fundamentals, valuation and business risk.

item.title: Crude oil futures rebound and pushed back into positive territory
item.description:
Crude oil futures have rebounded after trading lower earlier in the day, with buyers defending a key cluster of technical support.

The low reached $91.70, just above the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the July low to the September high at $91.60. The price also held above the rising 100-hour moving average at $91.36 and the 200-hour moving average at $90.86.

That trifecta of support gives traders a clear area to define risk. Sellers would need to break below all three levels to shift the technical bias more firmly to the downside. Until then, buyers retain more control.

Buyers reclaim $93.48. Yesterday’s high is next.

The rebound has taken the price back above the top of a swing area at $93.48, with crude currently trading near $93.79. Staying above $93.48 would keep the immediate momentum tilted higher.

The next target is yesterday’s high at $94.36. A break above that level would open the door toward the late-September highs near $96.50, followed by the swing area between $97.00 and $98.48.

What would give sellers more control?

A move back below $93.48 would weaken the rebound, but sellers would still need to work through the support cluster between $91.60 and $90.86.

A break below that area would put Monday’s low near $89.60 in focus, followed by the September swing low at $88.72. Below those levels, traders would look toward the 50% midpoint of the July-to-September rally at $86.91, which was tested on October 6.

For now, sellers had their shot near the retracement support and could not push through. Buyers have regained some momentum. The next challenge is to hold above $93.48 and extend through $94.36.

Trading lesson: Use technical levels to define risk

When a Fibonacci retracement and moving averages sit close together, they create a cluster of support. That gives traders a clear area to judge whether buyers are holding control or sellers are gaining ground.

For crude oil, that area runs from $91.60 down to $90.86. Holding above it supports the bullish bias. Breaking below it—and staying below—would strengthen the sellers’ case.

The lesson is to let the price action guide you. Support gives buyers a place to lean against and define risk, but it does not guarantee a bounce. Know what would prove your trade wrong before you enter.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

Prices declined in all four regions during September. Compared with last year, the Northeast recorded the strongest increase, while the West was the only region with lower prices. These price figures are not seasonally adjusted, so monthly declines can reflect normal seasonal patterns.

September existing-home sales by region — seasonally adjusted annualized rates:

  • Northeast: 470,000 vs 480,000 in August, down 2.1% MoM. Down 4.1% YoY from 490,000 last September.
  • Midwest: 930,000 vs 930,000 in August, unchanged MoM. Down 2.1% YoY from 950,000.

  • National: 3.99 million vs 3.93 million in August, up 1.5% MoM. Down 2.2% YoY from 4.08 million.

The South and West drove September’s monthly gain. However, sales remained below last September in every region, with the West recording the largest annual decline.

Annualized means the monthly sales pace is expressed as a yearly rate, after adjusting for seasonal patterns. It is not the actual number of homes sold during the year.

US existing-home sales increased 1.5% in September, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). The gain offers some encouragement, but the broader picture remains soft. August and September were the two slowest months for sales this year on a seasonally adjusted basis.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said recent increases in mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to qualify. Meanwhile, higher inventory and longer selling times mean sellers may need to offer price discounts or other incentives. Buyers have more negotiating power, but financing remains a hurdle.

Quick analysis:Sales moved higher, but one monthly gain does not establish a recovery. Annual declines across all four regions point to continued weakness. Softer housing demand could weigh on growth and support lower yields at the margin, although this report alone is unlikely to change the Federal Reserve’s policy outlook.

What this report measures:Existing-home sales track completed purchases of previously owned homes, including single-family houses, condominiums and co-ops. The headline sales level is seasonally adjusted and annualized, meaning it expresses the monthly pace as a yearly rate. Traders watch the report for clues about housing demand and the impact of mortgage rates.

item.title: Gold rebounds after the run to the 100 and 200 hour MAs found buyers
item.description:
Yesterday, I did a post-on gold sellers on the back of news Kazakhstan was selling some of the reserves. I spoke cautiously in regard to the move given the semi-holiday trading, but acknowledged that the precious metal was testing a key target near the 100 and 200 hour moving averages and that the area would help define the next move.

See the post and the video HERE

Gold buyers ended up defending the  important technical area. The price has bounced higher in trading here today but those buyers still have work to do before claiming more control.

The pullback tested the 100-hour and 200-hour moving averages (blue and green lines on the chart below), where willing buyers helped stall the decline. The price has since bounced above those levels and is trading near $4,184 in the supplied chart. That is good news for the buyers. The next challenge is getting above and staying above the resistance overhead.

Hourly moving averages define the risk

The two hourly moving averages are nearly on top of each other:

  • 100-hour moving average: $4,157.82
  • 200-hour moving average: $4,157.78

That makes the area near $4,158 the immediate support barometer. Stay above, and buyers keep the recovery alive. It also gives traders a level where risk can be defined and limited.

Move below and stay below, however, and the support defense loses its significance. Sellers would regain more control, with attention turning back toward the recent lows.

Buyers still face an important ceiling

On the topside, the next key hurdle is the swing area between $4,223.51 and $4,237.55. That area has acted as both support and resistance on a number of occasions going back to June.

The 61.8% retracement at $4,229.43 sits inside that zone, adding another technical reason to pay attention when the price gets there.

Buyers have defended support, but they have not broken the ceiling. Getting above and staying above the swing area would be a more meaningful step toward stronger upside control.

Just above that zone is the 100-day moving average at $4,252.80. Buyers need to clear that level as well to strengthen the broader recovery. If they succeed, the next target would be the 50% retracement at $4,318.18.

Conversely, if sellers lean against those resistance levels and the price rotates lower, the rally would remain a recovery within the larger decline from the late-August high.

Trading education: Holding support is step one

This setup illustrates why traders should separate a successful support test from a confirmed change in the broader bias.

Holding the hourly moving averages tells us buyers are willing to defend that area. It does not automatically tell us they can overcome the sellers waiting above.

The sequence is straightforward:

  • Hold above the hourly moving averages to preserve the recovery.
  • Clear the swing area to overcome a repeatedly tested ceiling.
  • Get above and stay above the 100-day moving average to strengthen the bullish bias.

A brief move through resistance is only the first step. If the price cannot stay above it, sellers have a reason to lean against the level again. The follow-through matters.

For now, support near $4,158 keeps buyers in the near-term battle, while $4,223.51–$4,237.55 and $4,252.80 remain the upside hurdles. The price action will provide the next clue.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin sellers had a go but could not push the lower targets
item.description:
Bitcoin moved lower yesterday, breaking below its 100-hour moving average and approaching the bottom of the swing area at $81,183. The low reached $81,388, falling short of that key downside target before buyers stepped back in.

Sellers had their shot. They missed.

The rebound subsequently carried the price above the 100-hour moving average at $82,997 and the 200-hour moving average at $83,545. However, buyers could not sustain the upside momentum. The price has since slipped back between those two technical levels.

Moving averages become the barometers

With bitcoin sandwiched between the hourly moving averages, traders have clear levels to define risk and judge who is taking control:

  • Above the 200-hour MA at $83,545: The bias becomes more bullish. Buyers would then look toward resistance near $84,236, corresponding with Monday’s high and today’s high area. Getting above—and staying above—that level would give the rebound more credibility.

  • Below the 100-hour MA at $82,997: The bias shifts back toward the sellers. The downside focus returns to yesterday’s low at $81,388 and the swing-area floor at $81,183. Below that, the September 19 low at $80,106 becomes the next key target.

For beginner traders, the distinction is between crossing a moving average and holding beyond it. Today’s rebound crossed both averages, but the failure to stay above the 200-hour MA shows that buyers still have work to do.

The broader range still needs a shove

Bitcoin has been trading up and down within a broader range since September 18. The key boundaries remain $80,106 on the downside and $87,374 on the upside.

A sustained break beyond either extreme would signal that the market is finally resolving that consolidation. Until then, the 100- and 200-hour moving averages act as the nearer-term barometers within the range.

The sellers failed to reach their downside target. The buyers have responded, but have yet to establish control.

Be patient. Listen to the price action and the clues from the technical tools. Then wait for the next shove.

Trading lesson: A failed move creates an opportunity, but confirmation still matters

When sellers push toward support but cannot break through, traders should pay attention. That failure can trigger a rebound as sellers exit and buyers step in. However, a bounce alone does not mean buyers are in control.

That is where the moving averages help:

  • Stay above the 200-hour MA at $83,545: Buyers have a stronger case for further upside.

  • Move back below the 100-hour MA at $82,997: The rebound loses credibility, and sellers regain the advantage.

  • Remain between the averages: The market is still deciding. Be patient and wait for the next shove.

The lesson is to use technical levels to define your risk, judge the bias, and recognize when your trade idea is no longer working. You do not need to predict every move. You need to know what the price must do to support your view—and what would tell you that you are wrong.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Silver trims losses as oil prices ease, but downside risks persist; focus turns to US CPI for potential relief rally

item.title: Is the AI bubble bursting?
item.description:
Nostradamus has been dead for centuries, but his followers are still around, especially in finance, with Ray Dalio warning that the AI bubble may be close to bursting as interest rates rise and tech companies take on massive debt to build AI infrastructure.

Are we heading for another dot-com crash?

Things do seem to be getting murkier for the sector, with OpenAI’s annualized revenue reaching around $50 billion at the end of September, $20 billion below the previously expected $70 billion. As concerns grow that AI demand may be slowing and revenues may not justify massive infrastructure investments, Oracle, Microsoft, and Nvidia shares, alongside the Nasdaq-100, have naturally come under pressure. 

This week, selling pressure also spread to semiconductor and tech stocks across Asian markets. Chinese chipmaker CXMT’s progress in developing a new memory architecture has raised concerns about growing competition for global memory makers. On top of that, Broadcom’s CEO compared AI investors to casino gamblers, suggesting some don’t fully understand what they’re betting on, and warned that financing AI infrastructure could become a major challenge.

Looking ahead, high Treasury yields could add fuel to the fire by making riskier AI stocks less attractive to investors. 

Still, this isn’t a classic bubble, as massive infrastructure spending is backed by real growth in revenue, orders, and contract backlogs. Microsoft’s Azure, for example, has surpassed $100 billion in annual revenue, AWS has posted its fastest growth in years, and Celestica and AMD are also seeing strong demand for AI infrastructure. 

In other words, unlike in a typical bubble, companies aren’t betting on demand that may never materialize. They’re trying to keep up with demand that already exceeds capacity. At the same time, tech giants remain highly profitable and have ample cash to fund record investments without seriously risking their financial stability.

Still, the risks remain, as these massive investments have yet to pay off and high valuations — exceeding $2 trillion in the case of the upcoming Anthropic IPO — leave the sector vulnerable to growth disappointments, making this an important factor to consider when shaping your investment strategy. 

The next big test for the sector will be earnings season. By the way, this week, besides JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Citigroup, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley, and BlackRock, ASML and TSMC will also report, giving us a better idea of whether the AI boom still has legs. 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.description:
The U.S. dollar is lower after yesterday’s rise, with Treasury yields easing as the U.S. bond market returns from the Columbus Day holiday. Oil is also backing away from yesterday’s elevated levels, although the Middle East headlines continue to keep traders on alert.

For traders, the question is whether today’s dollar pullback can develop into something more. A rebound against the dollar is a start. Holding support and breaking the next resistance levels would give that move more credibility.

The dollar is lower across the major currencies

The greenback is lower against all seven major currencies, with its largest decline against the New Zealand dollar.

From the dollar’s perspective:

  • Against the NZD: down approximately 0.43%, with NZDUSD at 0.5610.

  • Against the CAD: down approximately 0.21%, with USDCAD at 1.4252.

The direction is consistent across the board. The next test is whether those gains against the dollar can hold through the North American session.

U.S. stocks: Dow higher, Nasdaq lower

At 8:12 AM ET, U.S. stock futures were implying a mixed market with the flow of funds into the industrials while the riskier Nasdaq stocks are lower:

  • Dow industrial average: up 393 points.

  • S&P 500: down 5 points.

  • Nasdaq 100: down 254 points.

The divergence is clear. The Dow is pointing higher, while technology remains under pressure. Earnings and company outlooks will help determine whether that split continues after the opening bell.

Earnings: Beats and misses

The US earnings season is kicking off today with the traditional financials leading the way.  Goldman, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo have released along with J&J and UnitedHealth:

  • Goldman Sachs — beat earnings and revenue. EPS of $17.01 exceeded $13.07 expected. Revenue of $18.7 billion topped the $16.84 billion estimate.

  • JPMorgan Chase — missed earnings and revenue. Reported EPS of $5.57 fell short of $5.93 expected. Revenue of $50.2 billion missed the $51.23 billion estimate. However, the bank raised its full-year net interest income outlook to $106.2 billion, above both the previous $105.5 billion guidance and the $105.28 billion estimate.

  • Wells Fargo — beat earnings, missed revenue and net interest income. EPS of $1.87 topped $1.85 expected. Revenue of $21.9 billion missed the $22.31 billion estimate, while net interest income of $12.5 billion fell short of $12.7 billion expected.

  • Johnson & Johnson — missed adjusted earnings; revenue was slightly above forecast. Adjusted EPS of $2.59 missed the feed’s $2.67 estimate. Revenue of $25.4 billion was just above $25.38 billion expected. The company raised its full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $11.05–$11.15, from $10.96–$11.11.

  • UnitedHealth — beat earnings and revenue, with guidance above expectations. Adjusted EPS of $4.69 exceeded $4.12 expected. Revenue of $112.7 billion topped $111.31 billion expected. Full-year adjusted EPS is now projected at at least $20.50, versus $19.80 expected.

The lesson for traders is to look beyond the headline EPS number. Revenue, lending income and forward guidance can change how investors interpret a beat or a miss.

Korean chipmakers lead a sharp selloff

  • South Korea’s Kospi fell 5.46%.

The selling centered on the country’s semiconductor heavyweights:

  • Samsung Electronics: down approximately 7.4%.

  • SK Hynix: down approximately 10.1%.

Reports of advances at Chinese memory-chip producer CXMT raised concerns about competition for Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron. That added to broader unease over the AI investment boom. The Kospi recovered some ground after falling more than 7% intraday.

For the chipmakers, the concern is what increased competition could mean for pricing power and profit margins. Strong demand can continue, but investors also need confidence that the companies can maintain the earnings that support their valuations.

Treasury yields move lower

U.S. Treasury yields are lower as cash bond trading resumes:

  • 2-year:4.770%, down approximately 2.1 basis points.

  • 5-year:4.974%, down approximately 4.7 basis points.

  • 10-year:5.187%, down approximately 5.7 basis points.

  • 30-year:5.551%, down approximately 5.4 basis points.

The pullback in yields accompanies the softer dollar, but the 10-year remains above 5%. Tomorrow’s inflation report will be an important test of whether yields can continue to ease.

Fed commentary: AI spending and inflation

Austan, president of the Chicago Fed, warned that inflation remains too high and that AI-related demand may be spreading price pressures beyond data centers and their immediate suppliers. He described employment and consumer spending as solid, while expressing concern about broader overheating demand.

Christopher, a Fed governor, said the U.S. remains dominant in building AI models and that hyperscalers still plan substantial investment over the next three years. He also said higher yields could do some of the Fed’s work by restraining demand.

The policy question is whether AI investment raises productive capacity quickly enough to offset the demand and cost pressures created during the buildout.

RBA minutes keep further hikes on the table

The RBA’s September meeting minutes showed unanimous agreement that a 25-basis-point hike was necessary, taking the cash rate to 4.60%.

The board was concerned that excess demand was greater than previously assumed and that inflation could remain elevated. Higher oil prices, domestic cost pressures and signs of AI-related price pressures were among the concerns. The RBA reiterated that it would raise rates further if needed.

There is also evidence of strain. Australian business confidence fell to -13 in September, while business conditions held at -1. That leaves the RBA balancing weak confidence against persistent inflation pressures.

Oil and the Middle East remain key drivers

Oil is lower this morning, but the underlying geopolitical risks remain. Saudi Arabia has vowed a response to Houthi attacks, while U.S.-Iran negotiations remain stalled. Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have added another source of uncertainty.

Saudi Arabia is also examining ways to increase its ability to move crude through pipelines. Converting a gas pipeline could add approximately 1.2 million barrels per day of capacity within seven to eight weeks, according to the Saudi energy minister. That could ease some transport concerns, although execution and security risks remain.

For markets, oil matters through the inflation channel. Renewed gains could keep pressure on yields and rate expectations. A sustained retreat would ease some of that pressure.

The calendar: Fed speakers today, CPI tomorrow

Today’s scheduled events include:

  • 8:00 AM ET: OPEC’s monthly oil market report.

  • 10:00 AM ET: Austan, president of the Chicago Fed, speaks.

  • 1:00 PM ET: Tom Barkin, president of the Richmond Fed, speaks.

  • 4:00 PM ET: Susan Collins, president of the Boston Fed, speaks.

The bigger scheduled economic risk is Wednesday’s U.S. CPI report, with PPI and retail sales also ahead this week. Those reports will help traders assess inflation pressures and the strength of consumer demand.

EURUSD: Buyers try to extend the rebound

EURUSD is trading near 1.1187, toward the upper end of its 1.1154–1.1196 session range. The gains come after the pair moved to new lows for the year yesterday in the holiday trading.  

The session high at 1.1196 is the immediate upside reference and is also near its 100 hour MA at 1.1193 currently. A break above it, followed by an ability to stay above, would give the rebound more momentum with the 200 hour MA at 1.1216 the next key target to get to and through. .

On the downside, 1.1154 is the session’s lower boundary. Buyers need to show they can hold higher levels rather than allow the rebound to unwind.

USDJPY: Sellers press toward the session low

USDJPY is trading near 158.13, below the session high at 158.66 and closer to the low at 157.84.

A break below 157.84 would extend the session’s dollar weakness. Failure to break and hold below that level would leave room for a rebound within the range.

The session high at 158.66 remains the upper reference for today’s trading.

GBPUSD: Buyers approach the session high

A move above 1.3246 would open the door to a range extension. The buyers would then need to hold that break to show they have more control.

The session low at 1.3205 defines the lower boundary. A reversal toward that level would weaken the recovery.

item.title: Long global semiconductors remains the most crowded trade followed by short US Treasuries, according to Bank of America
item.description:
The latest Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey showed investors have become less optimistic about the macroeconomic outlook, while positioning in technology stocks remains near its most extreme level in six years. The survey was conducted between October 2 and October 8 among 161 participants managing $453 billion in assets.

The Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey (FMS) is one of the most influential monthly reports in the financial world. It polls roughly 200 to 400 institutional fund managers (people managing hundreds of billions of dollars in hedge funds, pension funds, and mutual funds) to see how they are positioned in the markets.

The survey is often used as a contrarian indicator because extreme positioning can reveal where consensus trades are vulnerable to disappointment. However, crowded positioning alone is not a sufficient reason to bet against a trend. The opportunities come when stretched positioning coincides with a catalyst that changes market expectations.

Fund managers are now more overweight technology stocks than at any point since August 2020. The proportion of respondents overweight the sector increased to 37% from 30% in September, while global semiconductors remain the most crowded trade. At the same time, investors have made their largest reduction in bank exposure since March 2023. Although sentiment has weakened, investors are still broadly positive on the macroeconomic outlook. That leaves equities vulnerable if economic activity or corporate earnings disappoint.

The survey showed a disorderly rise in bond yields as the biggest tail risk to markets, followed by an AI bubble. Short US Treasuries is the second-most crowded trade. If inflation moderates or economic growth deteriorates, Treasury yields could fall and force investors to unwind bearish bond positions.

Moreover, for the first time in several months, investors have started to turn negative on the global growth outlook. A net 4% now expect the global economy to weaken over the next 12 months. Further deterioration in growth expectations could weigh on stock markets and lead to a fall in Treasury yields. 

The US midterm elections on November 3 are approaching amid elevated energy prices, inflation concerns and geopolitical tensions. Investors are expecting a Democratic House and Republican Senate, while 31% expect a Democratic sweep. In the latter scenario, 32% expect bond yields to rise and equities to fall, while 22% anticipate a fall in yields and stocks. 

Prediction markets have increasingly favoured a Democratic sweep, as election expectations continue to evolve amid macro and geopolitical developments. A Democratic sweep has certainly become more likely given the mess caused by Trump since last year.

Keep in mind, that even a Democratic sweep wouldn't change much as Trump would retain the power to continue the Iran war or impose tariffs. It could reduce fiscal fears though, supporting long-term bonds and leading to a fall in Treasury yields. The stock market might react positively initially if Treasury yields fall, but going forward, the US-Iran war and deteriorating growth expectations could drag it down to new lows.

item.title: Connecting the dots: How the AI boom could turn into the Fed's next inflation headache
item.description:
Here's some food for thought. What if I told you that amid all the excitement about AI and how it is transforming our lives, some of that could eventually show up on your electricity bill? That would be interesting, no?

Let's break it down and take a look at how that might turn out to be the case in reality.

Now, when we talk about AI, we tend to imagine smarter chatbots, robot innovation, and tech stocks taking off to the moon. However, there's a much less glamorous side to all of that. I mean, somebody has to be the one to build enormous buildings to house all those computers, and then also keep them running around the clock. Yes, I'm talking about data centres here. And these buildings need electricity to work and cooling systems to stop them from overheating.

So, picture this. You have tens of these buildings now suddenly turning up in the same town; that is in fact what is happening across the globe. Now, the local power grid wasn't necessarily built for that much demand in mind. As such, the utility company might have to bring in more power, upgrade substations and lay new cables. Those things are not cheap. And depending on how some of those costs are shared, some of the bill could end up with households and businesses.

And it's not just electricity, either. These projects need plenty of raw material like steel and copper, alongside specialised equipment and skilled construction workers. If the tech giants are scrambling for the same supplies and contractors all at once, those prices can get pushed even higher.

I wouldn't blame you for thinking that we are talking about some distant hypothetical situation here. But not quite. Dallas Fed researchers had earlier this year estimate that the impact of data centres on electricity prices alone could add around 0.04 to 0.13 percentage points to annual US inflation by 2030 under plausible scenarios.

Now, that estimate isn't exactly an inflation crisis by itself. But with the Fed already in a massive struggle to get inflation back to 2%, it is just another potential headache to deal with.

And this is all before considering the fact that we could also see businesses start passing higher power and building costs on to customers. That will just be another reason for the Fed to consider tighter monetary policy amid the "higher for longer" narrative. That could also keep Treasury yields elevated, putting more pressure on expensive tech stocks. Quite the irony, no?

Of course, there is also the other side of the argument. AI could also make businesses more efficient and bring costs down over time. I don't doubt that. But while the promise is to make things cheaper and more efficient, the road to get there could prove to be rather expensive.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: EUR/CHF bounces this week but French bond spreads warn euro risks aren't over
item.description:
The euro appears to be catching a bit of a break against the franc this week, though I'm not entirely convinced that the danger has passed just yet.

EUR/CHF was pressured late last week and tested waters below the 0.9300 level, posting its weakest daily close since July. But as we get into the new week, the pair managed to bounce off the key technical region around 0.9300 with the 100-day moving average (red line) and trendline support from the March and May lows helping to provide an additional layer of defense for buyers.

So, the question now is whether buyers can build on that rebound or if this is merely a temporary reprieve.

For now, the cluster of support levels around the 0.9300 region remains the key line in the sand. A firm break below that would put the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 0.9236 in focus next, before potentially opening up a move towards the 0.9200 level.

The key risk for the currency pair? It is the fact that the French-German bond yield spread continues to stay elevated around 141 bps, not far from the recent highs near 150 bps.

The wider yield spread suggests that investors are still demanding a hefty premium to hold French debt, with fiscal concerns continuing to outweigh confidence. And the longer that this situation persists, the greater the risk that some of the unease we're seeing could spill over into other euro area bond markets.

For now, we're certainly not quite at the stage to label this as another euro area debt crisis. However, it is a warning signal that I wouldn't want to be ignoring.

And with the US CPI report coming up tomorrow, that might be another potential catalyst to watch. A hotter-than-expected inflation reading could push Treasury yields higher and weigh on broader risk sentiment, potentially renewing demand for the franc. At the same time, that could drive a further selloff in global bond markets as well and drag yields in Europe higher - further exacerbating the fiscal risks associated with French debt.

On the flip side, a softer report could offer EUR/CHF some light breathing room as seen with the calmer start to the new week so far. But even then, it won't make France's fiscal troubles disappear overnight.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
